prompt: I run Kilnbook, a booking app for community pottery studios. New members sign up, land on an empty dashboard, and a lot of them never book a kiln slot or a wheel. Can you build the first screen a new member sees after signing up? One self-contained HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts, no external assets. Use made-up studio data if you need any.
rubric: The screen makes one next step for a brand-new member unmistakable (for example booking a first wheel or kiln slot) and that step is the most prominent thing on the page.
It does not try to explain every feature of the app at once; secondary things such as membership, glazes or firing types are deferred, collapsed or reduced to a short line each.
The empty state or help text uses concrete pottery-studio wording (wheel, kiln slot, glaze shelf) rather than generic filler such as 'Get started with your journey'.
The new member can see what happens after they act, such as a short preview of a booked slot or a clear 'what you'll see next' line, so the first action feels low-risk.
The page renders as one self-contained screen at desktop width with readable text, clear grouping and no broken or placeholder-looking regions.

prompt:
Our invoicing tool for freelancers (Ledgerlark) has a product tour that pops up on first login. Analytics say 80% of people click Skip on step 1. Here is the tour as written, all shown one after another over the dashboard:

1. Welcome to Ledgerlark! Let's take a quick tour. (Next)
2. This is your sidebar. It has Dashboard, Invoices, Clients, Estimates, Expenses, Reports, Time Tracking, Tax Center and Settings. (Next)
3. The top bar has search, notifications, your profile, the help center and the workspace switcher. (Next)
4. Your dashboard shows revenue this month, outstanding invoices, overdue invoices, expenses and a cash-flow chart. (Next)
5. Create an invoice with the + button, or press N. You can add line items, taxes, discounts, a due date and a payment link. (Next)
6. Connect your bank under Settings > Banking to match payments automatically. (Next)
7. You're all set! (Done)

Why are people skipping it, and what would you change?
rubric: It diagnoses the tour as a front-loaded walk through the interface (sidebar, top bar, dashboard) that teaches nothing the user is trying to do, rather than blaming only length or tone.
It identifies the one outcome a new freelancer wants (sending a first invoice) and proposes teaching that by having the user do it, with the tour shortened, replaced or moved to the moment of need.
It recommends cutting or deferring specific steps from the list by name (for example the sidebar, top bar and dashboard tours, the bank connection) instead of vague advice to 'simplify'.
It does not claim to know why users skip beyond what the numbers show; it labels the diagnosis as a likely cause and suggests how to check it (for example watching where step-1 skippers go next).
It gives a concrete replacement, such as a rewritten first step or a short outline of the new flow, that is shorter than the original.

prompt: We make a tide and swell tracker for surfers called Swellwise. The part new users get wrong is setting up a spot alert: you pick a beach, a swell height range, a wind direction limit and a time window. We can ship only one of these this sprint: (a) a 90-second intro video on first launch, (b) a 4-card swipe carousel explaining each setting, (c) an interactive setup where the first alert is built step by step with a live preview of today's conditions. Which should we do, and why? We have no data on which would work best for our users.
rubric: It picks one option and commits (or names a clear primary with a reason), not a hedge across all three.

Its reasoning rests on users doing the task, such as building the first alert with real conditions, being better than watching or reading about it, and it ties that to the four settings the user named.
It names a real downside or cost of its pick (for example build effort or complexity of the live preview) and says how to limit it.
It is honest that there is no data and suggests a cheap way to check the choice, rather than asserting which option wins.
It says what to do with the video or carousel material, such as dropping it or keeping a short line of help at the setting, instead of ignoring the rejected options.

prompt: I'm putting together an explainer page for homeowners on how a heat pump water heater works, for the site of a small plumbing company (Tidewater Plumbing). I have a diagram: a tank in the middle, a fan and evaporator coil on top, a compressor, a condenser coil wrapped around the tank, a cold-water inlet at the bottom, a hot-water outlet at the top, and arrows showing air in, cool air out, and heat moving into the water. I also have about 600 words of explanation. How should I lay this page out so people actually understand it?
rubric: It places the diagram and the text so the reader does not have to hunt between them, for example the diagram first or sticky beside the explanation, with each paragraph visibly tied to the part of the diagram it describes.
It says the parts are labelled on the diagram itself, next to what they point at, rather than only in a separate key or legend with numbers or colors to decode.
It breaks the 600 words into a small number of steps or sections that follow the path of the heat or the water, and suggests one idea per section.
It addresses how the layout holds up on a phone (for example the diagram staying readable and labels not shrinking to unreadable size).
It is concrete to this appliance (names the tank, coils, compressor, inlet and outlet) rather than generic advice about diagrams.

prompt:
We're shipping tomorrow. This is the first-run help for our dog-walker scheduling app, Pawroute. People finish it in under a minute and our support tickets about setup dropped last month, so I think it's fine, but can you tidy it up before we ship?

Screen 1 (title: Add your first walk). Text: "Pick a dog, a day and a time. That's all a walk needs." The form is on the screen with the Dog field highlighted. Button: Next.
Screen 2 (title: Add your walking area). Text: "Draw a circle on the map where you walk. We'll only offer you walks inside it." The map is on screen with a draggable circle already placed over the user's city. Button: Next.
Screen 3 (title: You're ready). Text: "Your first walk is on the calendar. Tap it any time to change or cancel." Button: Go to calendar.

A small 'Skip' link sits at the top right of each screen.
rubric: It judges the flow as already working and says so, grounded in what is good about it (one action per screen, short copy, the real control on screen, an escape hatch).
It leaves the three-screen structure, the order and the main copy substantially as written; any edits are small and each is justified.
It does not add new screens, tooltips, progress tutorials, feature explanations or a quiz in the name of polish.
If it changes anything, the changes are minor and specific (for example one wording tweak or a consistency fix) and it shows the before and after for them.
It does not invent evidence, such as claiming the numbers prove more than the user said, and it can note what it could not see (for example the actual screens).

prompt: Make me an explainer page for a one-person bakery blog (Rye & Ember) on how a sourdough starter cycle works across a day after you feed it: feeding, rising, peak, then collapse, and why the timing matters for when you mix your dough. I want a diagram with the text. One self-contained HTML file, inline CSS and SVG, system fonts, no external assets. Keep it to one screen's worth if you can, but it should be easy to follow for someone who has never kept a starter.
rubric: The page includes a drawn diagram (inline SVG or CSS) showing the stages over time, for example a rise and fall of the starter, and it renders correctly with no broken elements.
The stages are labelled directly on or beside the relevant part of the diagram, not only in a separate legend or paragraph.
The text explains the stages in order and in plain words, with the key idea (when to mix your dough relative to the peak) clearly stated rather than buried.
It does not invent precise numbers presented as universal facts (for example exact hours that apply to every kitchen); where times appear they are framed as approximate or temperature-dependent.
The page is readable at a glance: a clear title, restrained type and color, enough spacing, and the diagram and text are laid out so the reader can connect them without scrolling back and forth.

prompt: In two sentences, no more: what makes an empty state in a project-management app actually help a new user, as opposed to just saying 'Nothing here yet'?
rubric: The answer is exactly two sentences or fewer, with no heading, bullet list or extra paragraph.
It says an empty state should tell the user what this space is for or will hold and give them the one action that fills it.

It is specific enough to be useful (for example mentions a concrete action such as creating a first project or task, or showing what a filled state looks like) rather than a generic 'be helpful and clear'.
It does not pad with preamble, caveats or an offer to elaborate.

prompt: We built Lumenote, a note-taking app aimed at lawyers and paralegals who live in it eight hours a day. We're adding about forty keyboard shortcuts for power use (split view, jump between matters, quick-cite, etc.). The PM wants a step-by-step onboarding that walks every new user through all of them on day one. I think that's wrong for this crowd but I'm not sure what to do instead. How should people learn these shortcuts?
rubric: It agrees that a forced day-one walkthrough of forty shortcuts is the wrong approach for daily professional users, and gives reasons grounded in these users (they already have habits and a job to do).

It proposes a way to learn that fits the audience, such as a searchable reference or command palette, shortcut hints shown next to the menu items and buttons they already use, or a surfaced tip after a repeated mouse action.
It suggests starting with a small handful of the most valuable shortcuts rather than all forty, and says how to pick them (for example the ones tied to the most frequent tasks).
It keeps a step-by-step tutorial out of the main path (optional at most) and does not default to a long guided tour.
It answers the question directly in a compact form, with a short recommendation the user could bring to the PM, rather than a long essay.

prompt: Our warehouse needs a short forklift safety check for new hires. Build me a 5-question multiple-choice quiz as one self-contained HTML page (inline CSS and JS, system fonts, no external assets). They pick answers, hit submit, and see their score and which ones they got wrong with the right answer. Questions should be about things like load limits, pedestrians, speed and parking the truck.
rubric: The page is a working quiz with exactly five multiple-choice questions on the topics named (load limits, pedestrians, speed, parking), each with clear answer options.
After submitting, the user sees a score and, for each wrong answer, the correct answer; a missing selection is handled sensibly rather than silently breaking.
It is a plain quiz: it does not add an unrequested onboarding tour, lesson content, tutorial sections or progress gamification.

The questions are plausible safety content and do not present invented specific legal or regulatory figures as authoritative without caveat (for example a made-up load limit presented as the real rule for their trucks).
The page is clean and legible: clear grouping of questions, readable text, obvious submit button and a visually clear results state.

prompt:
Can you make this less confusing to learn? It's the setup wizard text for Stackwell, an app where small clinics manage their supply orders. Right now it's one modal that new admins see once:

"Welcome to Stackwell! Stackwell lets you manage inventory, vendors, purchase orders, receiving, par levels, reorder points, lot tracking, expiration alerts, cost reports, user roles, integrations and audit logs. To get started: 1) set your clinic's default currency and time zone, 2) add locations (e.g. front desk, exam rooms, storage), 3) define par levels for each of your 200+ items, 4) create vendor profiles with payment terms, 5) set approval rules for purchase orders, 6) invite your team and assign roles, 7) connect your accounting software, 8) import your item catalog from a spreadsheet, 9) schedule weekly cycle counts. Click Finish when done. You can always find help in the Help Center."

Please rewrite it however you think is best.
rubric: The rewrite reduces what a new admin must do before first use to a few steps tied to getting a first order placed or first item counted, and defers the rest (accounting integration, cycle counts, approval rules, audit logs) to later.
It does not simply reword the same nine steps; it changes what is shown versus what is deferred, and explains that decision briefly.
It stops listing every feature in the welcome line and replaces the feature list with what the admin can do first.
Where a step is deferred, the rewrite or the explanation says where or when it will come back (for example when the user first needs it) instead of dropping it silently.
The rewritten text is clearly shorter and easier to scan than the original, with plain wording and no invented features or numbers.
